title: Revise the rule
hookLine: keep, cut, add: Moses cuts new stone for the same words, and the broken tablets ride along in the ark
tomorrow: can a whole rule be said while standing on one foot?

lines: HEW THEE TWO TABLES OF STONE.
cards: Somewhere there's a folder called "old": the first version of an essay, a song, a résumé, kept just in case. Moses had one, and it was made of stone.

He comes down the mountain carrying the tablets, and Exodus says they were the work of God. At the foot of the mountain, the people are dancing around a golden calf. He throws the tablets down and they break.
Later the word comes, in the King James Version: "Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first."

teach.b: So version two is different in one way and the same in another. The words stay: God will write on them "the words that were in the first tables, which thou brakest." But this time Moses cuts the stone himself.
Same words, new stone, his own hands. And the broken pieces? The Torah doesn't say.
In the tractates Berakhot and Bava Batra, the rabbis teach that the whole tablets and the broken tablets were both kept in the ark. The broken ones weren't swept away. They traveled with the people.
And the Talmud draws a teaching straight from it: honor an old scholar who has forgotten his learning, because the broken tablets also lay in the ark.
That's the Jewish thread here: what's broken is still holy, and still carried. And a detail worth keeping: by this reading, the ark held a broken version and a finished one, side by side.
So for your second version: keep what's true from the first. Cut what broke in the test week. Add what was missing.
And don't shred version one. It's the first stone, and it taught you how to cut the second.

how: The Talmud's teaching that the broken tablets were kept in the ark is cited as a reason to honor elders whose learning has faded. On a personal rule, a second version keeps, cuts and adds, and the first version can be kept rather than thrown away.

games.q: your grandfather, once a brilliant engineer, now loses his words mid-sentence. at dinner a cousin talks right over him. what does the Talmud's lesson of the tablets say?
o: honor him still: the broken tablets were kept in the ark too.
let him rest; the next generation should do the talking now.
correct him gently each time he gets a fact wrong.
games.why: the Talmud: honor an old scholar who has forgotten his learning, because the broken tablets also lay in the ark.

practice: Pick up your first version, or any page you've written on, and feel its weight in both hands. Fold it once, slowly, and set it down somewhere you keep things that matter.
Then rest your empty hands and let version two take shape: one thing kept, one cut, one added.

wordCard.voice: Revise the rule: keep, cut, add, and carry the old version with you. Like the second tablets: the same words on new stone.

orig.note: Hebrew: the broken tablets, kept in the ark in the Talmud's telling.

carryVoice: Something to keep: version two, cut from new stone, with version one kept beside it. Until tomorrow.
